I design the structure underneath complex products.

Senior product designer, nine years across fintech, carbon markets, broadcast media and automation. I founded and run my own studio, so I've taken products from the first conversation to the shipped release, the research, the information architecture, the permission models and the design system, and I prototype in code when that is the fastest way to answer a question.

I studied systems analysis before I studied design, so I reach for a model before I reach for a screen. I'm at my best where the problem is tangled: several kinds of user in one system, rules that change by role and region, decisions that are expensive to reverse.

How I work

UX as a strategic function, not a coat of paint.

I'm most useful early, where the problem is still being defined. My background in systems analysis means I think in structure: how a product is modelled, where the real constraints are, and what has to be true for people to trust it.

01

Frame before pixels

Research, information architecture and system modelling first. I make sure we're solving the right problem before anyone commits to a screen.

02

Design for everyone in the room

Most of what I build has more than one kind of user in it. A consumer, a partner store, a rep and a collaborator. A guest, an organiser, a sponsor. I model who can see what, who can approve what, and what gets logged, and I do it at wireframe stage, because getting it wrong later means rebuilding rather than restyling.

03

Decide what the machine may not decide

Most of my recent work is AI-shaped, and the design question is always the same one: which judgements the model is allowed to make, and which it has to hand back. Kodabase asks rather than guessing when a query is missing something it cannot infer. LawVerse is never permitted to write the page number. The interesting decision is almost always what you refuse to hand to the model.

04

Stay with it through release

I partner closely with engineering to the point where the thing is live, and I prototype in code when a working artifact answers a question faster than a mockup. Not because implementation is the job, but because a designer who has felt the cost of a decision in production specifies differently.

05

Write it down

Nine years of arguing the same points taught me to publish them instead. Three books, in two languages, and a habit of documenting the mechanics I would refuse to ship as carefully as the ones I would.

Background

Nine years, and how I ended up thinking this way.

I came to design through systems analysis, which is why I ask how a thing is modelled before I ask how it looks. Screens are the last decision, not the first.

The other half is motivation. I have spent years reading it properly, Octalysis, Maslow, McClelland, Herzberg, Max-Neef, and the useful part turned out not to be the mechanics you can add. It is the ones you can name and then refuse to add. My research file lists what I would not ship, and why, beside what I would. A leaderboard is not a feature, it is a claim about what your users want, and most of the time the claim is wrong.

I write, which is uncommon for a designer. Three books, in Portuguese and English. This year one of them got a new chapter on accessibility, because the European Accessibility Act turned good practice into law and a book about interface design without that chapter invites the question. My first piece of research, at university in 2015, was an access-control device that guided people who could not see it or hear it. That thread had been there longer than I realised.

Most of what I design now has a model somewhere inside it, and the question that keeps finding me is the same one every time: which judgements the system is allowed to make on its own, and which it has to hand back to a person. Kodabase asks instead of guessing when a query is missing something it cannot infer. LawVerse is allowed to say it does not know, and is never permitted to write the page number. That is the work I want more of.

And I build things nobody asked for, to think with. A reading platform, a browser game, an engine where characters carry memory and a body and go on living when the screen is closed. Not as a service I am selling, but because an idea gets tested there before it costs a client anything.

All work 01. Social · Product strategy · Design system

Next Day

An ephemeral social network for events, all the media from a night, organised and given back to you the day after.

Lead Product DesignerStrategy · UX · UI · Design systemB2B2C · iOSKolabs
The problem

At an event, the photos and videos are the real social currency, but they're scattered across WhatsApp, compressed, and gone within days. Nothing gives the collective experience back. The brief: turn a single night into a living, temporary social space, and return the memories to everyone who was there, the day after. Hence the name.

The hard part

Three known ways event apps die: download fatigue at the door, dead zones in a packed venue, and apps that fragment ticketing, access and content. Next Day had to be built against all three, while serving three very different users at once: the guest, the organiser, and the sponsor.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

Make the scarcity the product

Each event exists only while it happens, a live countdown, then releases its archive the next day.

Trade-off A short window to capture everything, in exchange for genuine urgency and a reason to return.
DECISION 02

One event = a full social feed

Profile, stories, reels and live channels (Backstage, VIP), a familiar, self-contained social world per event.

Trade-off More surface to design, in exchange for an experience guests already know how to use.
DECISION 03

One system, three intents

Guest (feed + subscription), organiser (media capture, challenges, monetisation), sponsor (brand challenges), modelled as one B2B2C system.

Trade-off Harder to model up front, but it avoids three disconnected products later.
DECISION 04

Built for the worst venue

Designed around saturated signal and download fatigue, entry by QR ties presence to place, and capture works when the venue doesn't.

Trade-off More states to handle, so the product survives real conditions.
What was designed

A dark, high-energy iOS app designed around the live event: QR entry, an event home with live channels and a countdown, an immersive full-screen media view, sponsor-backed challenges, and an organiser side for running it all.

Entry by QR (Decision 04), the event home (Decisions 01 & 02), and the immersive media view.

Challenges, how sponsors and organisers generate content, and the organiser's live event view (Decision 03).

A system, not a screen set

The depth is in the architecture behind the screens: a documented design system (foundations, components, roles, motion and voice), a 56-screen product map across five stakeholders, participant, organiser, artist, sponsor, staff, delivered as 117 hi-fi screens with their states, and a UI kit guiding the build.

The design system, the product inventory, and the UI kit, the architecture the app is built on.

Outcome & reflection

Next Day reframes a crowded space, "QR photo collection", into a different category: an ephemeral social layer with real monetisation for organisers and sponsors. What exists is the whole system rather than a set of screens, and that is what let a small team hold this much product in their heads at once.

It has not launched. The code is in three repositories and the design is finished, and the product has never met a real venue. I would rather say that plainly than dress a design decision up as a result. Everything below is what I learned building it, not what the market told me.

What I would carry forward: designing for the worst venue first changed the product, not just the states. Once you accept that the signal will be saturated and that nobody will download an app in a queue, entry by QR and capture-that-works-offline stop being edge cases and become the spine. Most event apps design the good conditions and then patch the bad ones, which is why they die at the door.

What I got wrong, or at least cannot defend yet: the entire product rests on scarcity, one night, then the archive. That is a strong hypothesis about behaviour and it is completely untested. If the countdown produces anxiety rather than urgency, the design does not degrade gracefully, it inverts. The first thing I would instrument is the gap between people who open the archive the next day and people who never come back.

All work 02. SaaS · White-label · Trust

Luckify

A white-label online-raffle platform, the "Hotmart of raffles", built with the mindset of a modern SaaS, in a category still running on outdated tech.

Product DesignerUX · UI · Dashboard · Design toolingWhite-label SaaSKolabs
The problem

Online raffles are big business in Brazil, but they run on technically mediocre platforms. Operators want their own branded storefront and real sales tools. Buyers, in a category full of scams, need to trust it at a glance. How do you make a raffle platform feel modern, credible, and genuinely good to sell with?

The hard part

Two audiences with opposite needs. The operator wants a powerful control panel and marketing tools. The buyer wants instant legitimacy. And it's white-label: every screen has to hold up when it's re-skinned to someone else's brand.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

Design a sales tool, not a raffle script

A data-informed dashboard, active raffles, numbers sold, sell-through, cost-per-acquisition and a "sells out in about three days" pacing forecast, that treats the operator like a business.

Trade-off More to design than a list of raffles, but it positions Luckify as high-value, not a commodity.
DECISION 02

White-label as a first principle

A component system that stays coherent and legible when recoloured to each operator's identity.

Trade-off Less bespoke per client, far more scalable across many brands.
DECISION 03

Trust as a visible surface

On the storefront, status and legitimacy are shown plainly, because the buyer's biggest fear is being scammed.

Trade-off Space spent on reassurance most competitors skip, but here it's the conversion.
DECISION 04

Tooling to scale the design itself

I built a Figma plugin to generate screens systematically, so the design keeps pace with the roadmap.

Trade-off Upfront tooling effort, repaid in speed and consistency.
What shipped

An operator dashboard built around real business metrics, a raffle-management view, and a clean buyer-facing storefront, one system, ready to wear any operator's brand.

Operator dashboard (Decision 01), raffle management, and the white-label storefront (Decisions 02 & 03).

Outcome & reflection

Luckify takes a category running on outdated tooling and gives operators something that looks and behaves like a serious modern SaaS, under their own brand. The deliverable is a component system that survives being recoloured for each operator, an operator dashboard built around business metrics rather than a list of raffles, and a buyer-facing storefront where legitimacy is stated instead of implied.

The decision I am most confident about is the least visible one: I built a Figma plugin to generate screens systematically rather than drawing them. In a white-label product the design debt compounds faster than anywhere else, because every inconsistency multiplies by the number of brands wearing it. Tooling was cheaper than discipline.

The decision I would test before defending: trust as a visible surface. I gave real estate to reassurance because the buyer's dominant fear in this category is being scammed, and I still believe that is right. But I designed it from reasoning, not from evidence. Nobody has measured whether the trust block moves conversion or just moves the fold, and in a category where competitors skip it entirely, "everyone else is wrong" is a claim that deserves a test rather than a paragraph.

Same for the pacing forecast. "Sells out in about three days" is useful only if the operator believes it, and an operator cannot inspect how it was calculated. A forecast people quietly stop trusting is worse than no forecast, and I did not design the explanation that would prevent that.

All work 03. Sustainability · Multi-sided platform

Carbono Neutro

An app that turns carbon neutralisation from an abstract idea into something you can calculate, pay for, and be rewarded for, with a benefits club at partner businesses.

Product DesignerResearch · IA · Multi-persona UX · UIApp & desktopcarbononeutro.app ↗
The problem

Most people accept that their consumption has a carbon cost, but it stays invisible: no number, no action, no reward. Offsetting is sold as a vague virtue. The brief was to make neutralisation concrete, affordable and habitual: something you actually do after a purchase, not something you intend to do one day.

The hard part

Two problems at once. First, abstraction: "carbon" means nothing until it's a number attached to your own spending. Second, a four-sided system: consumers, partner stores, collaborators and commercial representatives each needed a coherent product, sharing one design language, without collapsing into four disconnected apps.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

A calculator as the front door

Enter what you spent, choose how much to neutralise (3%–30%), pay by PIX or cash. The abstract becomes a number and a button.

Trade-off Simplifies complex emissions maths, in exchange for an action people actually complete.
DECISION 02

Reward the behaviour immediately

Every R$1 contributed earns a point, and points unlock a benefits club at partner businesses, plus NFT certificates of what you neutralised.

Trade-off More system than a donation flow, but it turns a one-off good deed into a habit.
DECISION 03

Make every contribution traceable

A statement lists each contribution, its value and the establishment it came from, credibility through transparency, in a sceptical category.

Trade-off Denser screens, but that is what turns a claim into evidence.
DECISION 04

One system, four roles

Consumer, partner store, collaborator and commercial representative each get their own dashboard, statement and profile, built from shared components.

Trade-off Heavier IA work up front, and one product to evolve instead of four.
What shipped

A multi-persona product: a neutralisation calculator with PIX payment, a consumer dashboard tracking contributions, carbon neutralised and NFTs earned, a fully traceable statement, and a partner-store dashboard with its own metrics and rewards.

The calculator (Decision 01), consumer dashboard (Decision 02), traceable statement (Decision 03) and partner-store view (Decision 04).

Outcome & reflection

Carbono Neutro is live. It turns offsetting into a two-minute action with a visible payoff, and gives partner businesses a commercial reason to take part rather than a moral one. Four roles, consumer, partner store, collaborator and commercial representative, each with a dashboard, a statement and a profile, all built from one shared component set.

The lesson I carry forward is the one the calculator taught: for behaviour to change, the abstract has to become a number, and the good deed has to pay something back the same day. "Carbon" means nothing. "You spent this, neutralise between 3 and 30 percent of it, pay by PIX" means something, and the traceable statement afterwards is what turns a claim into evidence in a category where nobody trusts a claim.

What I am not claiming: I designed the loop, I did not measure it. The benefits club is supposed to convert a one-off good deed into a habit, and whether it does is exactly the kind of thing that needs cohort data over months rather than a designer's confidence. If I picked one thing to instrument it would be second contributions, because a neutralisation product with no repeat rate is a donation form with extra steps.

And one decision I would revisit rather than defend. The NFT certificate made sense in the moment as proof of what you neutralised, and it now carries a reputational cost with exactly the environmentally-minded audience the product depends on. The underlying need was a verifiable receipt. The receipt was the requirement. The blockchain was a choice, and I would separate the two next time.

All work 04. Broadcast media · Civic platform

RIC

The audience app for a Brazilian television network, live polls, giveaways, comment threads and anonymous public reporting, all landing in one moderated newsroom inbox.

Product DesignerIA · Permission design · Wireframes → UIiOS & Androidric.com.br ↗
The problem

A regional broadcaster already had an audience talking to it, by WhatsApp, by social comments, by phone. But every channel arrived somewhere different, in a different format, with no record of who had answered what. Meanwhile the segments that most needed audience input, from a rural farming programme to local news, had no route back into the newsroom at all.

The brief looked like "build a second-screen app". The real problem was one inbox for everything the audience sends, and a newsroom that can safely work it.

The hard part

Two things made this harder than a comments feature.

First, anonymity with accountability. The most valuable thing a viewer can send a local broadcaster is also the most sensitive: a report about their own neighbourhood. People will only send it if they can stay anonymous, and a newsroom can only publish it if there is a trail showing who inside the organisation touched it.

Second, a network is not one place. RIC runs regional stations, and a report from one town is nobody's business in another. Permissions had to follow geography as well as seniority.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

Unify eight input types into one stream

Polls, giveaway entries, reports with photo and video, comments, media posts, report history, WhatsApp and event invitations all resolve into a single moderated feed rather than eight separate tools.

Trade-off A much heavier information architecture up front, in exchange for one product the newsroom learns once.
DECISION 02

Anonymous in, auditable inside

A report carries no identity outward, the detail screen simply reads Denunciante: Anônimo. Internally, two separate logs record what audiences did and what staff did to it.

Trade-off More build, and a harder conversation with legal. It is the only version a person actually risks using.
DECISION 03

Permissions on two axes, not one

Four roles by what they may do: Admin (delete), Editor (edit, redirect), Collaborator (reply), Viewer (view), crossed with two scopes: Master, which filters across every region, and Praça, which only ever receives its own region's traffic.

Trade-off Eight effective roles instead of four. It maps to how a broadcast network is actually staffed.
DECISION 04

Attach evidence, and put it on a map

Reports take photos and video as attachments and pin a location, so an editor can judge relevance before anyone is dispatched. Terms of use are accepted in the flow, not buried in settings.

Trade-off A longer submission than a text box, and the difference between a rumour and something publishable.
From wireframe to interface

Every screen was resolved in grey-box wireframes first, states, empty states, poll variants (single answer, multiple answer, partial result, closed) and the full report flow, before a single colour decision was made. The structure held. Only the surface changed.

Wireframes: a viewer's own report history, the report submission with attachments, and one of the poll variants.

What shipped

An audience app with four routes in the bottom bar, home, reports, polls, giveaways, and a fifth, VC com a RIC, that is the submission flow itself. Behind it, a newsroom console with role- and region-scoped moderation and two audit trails.

The anonymous report detail (Decisions 02 and 04), a programme feed with an inline poll, the live comment thread, giveaways with published winners, and the profile with its privacy controls.

Outcome & reflection

RIC gave a broadcaster something a comments section cannot: a channel where a viewer can report what is happening on their own street without putting their name to it, and a newsroom that can act on it with a record of who did what.

What I took from it is that moderation is a design problem, not an admin setting. The permission model, four verbs crossed with two geographic scopes, and separate logs for the public and for staff, was decided at wireframe stage, before any screen was styled. Getting that wrong later would have meant rebuilding the product, not restyling it.

All work 05. Consumer · Information architecture

Nomadic

An app for people who work from anywhere, and a rating system that asks whether a city is survivable, not whether it is fun.

Product DesignerIA · Taxonomy · Privacy designMobileDesigned end-to-end · not launched
The problem

Every product in this category rates cities the same way: cost of living, internet speed, how much fun it is. That set of questions describes a holiday. It does not describe what actually determines whether someone can live and work somewhere for three months.

The brief was an app for digital nomads, community, jobs, courses, places to work from. The interesting problem turned out to be much narrower: what should a city be rated on? Everything else in the product is downstream of that answer.

The hard part

Two things, and they pull against each other.

First, the honest version of the question is uncomfortable. "Is this city good?" is not one question, it is a different question depending on who is asking. A woman travelling alone, a same-sex couple, someone with a chronic condition and someone who just wants cheap coffee are not rating the same place.

Second, this product asks people to share where they are, what they do, and how to contact them, with strangers, in countries where some of those facts carry risk. Privacy could not be one switch.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

Rate lived risk, not lifestyle

41 rating categories instead of the usual five. Alongside cost and wifi sit safety at night, safe for women, safe for LGBTQ, drinkable tap water, air quality, political stability, dress code, and drug and alcohol regulation.

Trade-off A much heavier data model, and a rating people have to be persuaded to fill in, in exchange for a product that answers the question its users are actually asking.
DECISION 02

Privacy as four switches, not one

Profile, contact details, social links and profile-information sharing each get their own visibility setting: public, matches only, or hidden. Someone can be findable without being reachable.

Trade-off Four settings to explain instead of one, but a single toggle forces a choice between invisibility and exposure, which is no choice at all.
DECISION 03

Verify at the moment of contribution

Adding a place requires running a speed test in the form, not typing a number. The claim is measured where it is made.

Trade-off Slower to submit. The whole product's credibility rests on that one field being true.
DECISION 04

Reward the commons, not the ego

The badge that matters is Community Builder, add five new places with reliable internet. The gamification points at contributions the next person benefits from, not at streaks or vanity counts.

Trade-off Slower to trigger than a login streak, and less addictive. It grows the thing people came for.
The taxonomy

39 categories a city can be rated on. Highlighted are the ones that answer "can I exist here safely and legally", the questions the category standard leaves out.

Safety at NightSafe for WomenSafe for LGBTQPolitical StabilityDrinkable Tap WaterAir QualityQuality of HealthcareStrict Dress CodeDrug RegulationAlcohol RegulationAnti-Smoking LawsFriendly for ForeignersGeneral Safety Internet SpeedFree WiFiCost of LivingCost of AccommodationCost of FoodTaxesJob OpportunitiesQuality of EducationEase of Transportation24/7 ServicesClean CityQuiet PlaceNo InsectsLow CO2 EmissionsSustainableNatural AreasBeachNightlifeCultural DiversityRecreational ActivitiesFamily FriendlyPet FriendlyFood QualityTechnologyFree EventsPaid Events

Sorting runs on general rating, my preferences, or nomads' favourites, so the same 39 categories produce a different ranking per person rather than one league table.

Contact details are additionally gated on verification, and every match view carries Report and Block at the same level as Connect, not buried in an overflow menu.

The interface

Nomadic was taken all the way to high fidelity, onboarding, profile hub, matching and chat, a travel journal, travel plans and the jobs board, in a warm visual language built to feel like neither a corporate tool nor a dating app.

The screens below are a 2026 revisit of that surface. Same flows, same information, same feature set, nothing added and nothing removed. What changed is the visual language. Flat monoline icons in place of the 3D set, one deep accent instead of a bright gradient, left aligned type on a real scale, and photography where the original had none. Levels and badges came back as a progress ring around the avatar and an earned badge shelf, rather than shields floating beside a face.

The public profile with its level ring, the badge shelf further down it where one badge of twenty four is still locked (Decision 04), a match, the journal, the route, the jobs board, and a thread with the shared route underneath it. Photography is from Pexels, free for commercial use.

Outcome & reflection

Nomadic was specified in full, eleven feature areas, screen by screen, with states and filters, and designed to high fidelity across its core flows. The product never launched. What it left me with is the taxonomy, and the taxonomy is the point.

Deciding what a thing can be rated on is an act of deciding whose experience counts. The default set in this category quietly assumes a user for whom safety is not a variable. Adding safe for women and safe for LGBTQ to a rating form is a two-line change in a database and a completely different product.

What I would do differently: I wrote user testing into every one of the eleven feature areas and none of it happened. The personas behind this were archetypes derived from a player-type model, not people I interviewed. The taxonomy is a strong hypothesis. It is not yet a finding, and I would not present it as one.

Next case study

Kodabase →
All work 06. AI product · Data tooling

Kodabase

Ask your database a question in plain language. Four agents answer it, and the design work was deciding when they should stop and ask you something back.

Product owner & designerAI interaction · Schema UX · TrustWeb appKolabs
The problem

Natural-language querying demos beautifully and fails quietly. You type "show me sales last quarter", it writes SQL, it returns a number, and the number is wrong, because the model guessed which column meant what, and nothing in the interface ever told you it had guessed.

Real databases make this worse. They carry a decade of naming decisions made by people who have left: XZ_PERSON, USER_NAME, CLIENT_ID, some of which mean the same thing and some of which do not.

The hard part

An agent that admits uncertainty feels worse in a demo and is worth far more in use. Every clarifying question is friction, and friction is what a chat interface is supposed to remove. So the question was not whether to ask, it was which uncertainties are worth interrupting someone for, and which the system should carry silently.

The second problem: this product asks people to hand over live database credentials. Trust cannot be a paragraph in the terms.

The four agents
Orchestrator

Kore

Validates the prompt, resolves ambiguity with the user, assigns work to the others, and brings the answers back into one reply.

Query

Kquery

Turns the language into SQL, runs it, returns structured results, and logs every query and result for reuse.

Reporting

Kapture

Builds the charts, exports to PDF and Excel, and pins visualisations to the dashboard on request.

Schema

Kraft

Normalises the incoming schema, flags ambiguous names, and keeps a mapping from every old name to its new one.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

The agent asks rather than guesses

When a query is missing something it cannot infer, Kore stops and asks "What timeframe should I use for this query?" instead of choosing a default and reporting a confident number.

Trade-off A slower first answer, and a demo that looks less magical. It is the difference between a tool and a plausible-answer generator.
DECISION 02

Ambiguity is resolved with evidence, not a shrug

Kraft does not silently merge similar columns. It shows the user what it suspects and why: "The column 'XZ_PERSON' appears similar to 'CLIENT_ID'. Do they represent the same entity?"

Trade-off Setup takes longer. The alternative is a schema quietly reshaped by a guess nobody reviewed.
DECISION 03

Meaning is the one thing tests cannot check

Kraft keeps every old-to-new mapping, and surfaces it for correction. Not because automation needs supervising, tests and a security pass handle correctness downstream, but because whether XZ_PERSON means a client or a sales rep is not a fact any test can reach. It only exists in the user's head.

Trade-off One more screen. It is the narrow case where a human has information the pipeline structurally cannot obtain.
DECISION 04

Show the work while it happens

Chat reports what each agent is doing: "Kquery is retrieving data", "Kraft is analysing your schema", "Kapture generated a report in 15 seconds". The waiting state is where trust in a multi-agent system is won or lost.

Trade-off More surface to maintain, and it exposes the machinery. A spinner in front of four agents is just a spinner.
Asking, in practice
Kore
Show me sales by region last quarter
Kraft is analysing your schema…
KoreBefore I run this, the column XZ_PERSON looks similar to CLIENT_ID. Do they represent the same entity?
No, XZ_PERSON is the sales rep
KoreUnderstood. And "last quarter", calendar quarter, or your fiscal quarter starting in July?
Fiscal
Kquery is retrieving data…
KaptureReport generated in 15 seconds. Pin this chart to your dashboard?

Two questions before the first answer. Both are questions no model can resolve from the schema alone, and both would have produced a confidently wrong number if guessed.

Traceability

Every normalisation is recorded as a pair, so the original database stays legible and a semantic mistake can be caught by the one party who can catch it.

Old name  →  Normalised
USER_NAME  →  UserName
CLIENT_ID  →  ClientID
XZ_PERSON  →  PersonID

Credentials are encrypted the moment they are entered, and the interface is required to say so, at the point of entry and again on success. Security that the user cannot see does not buy the trust it paid for.

The screens

From the Kolabs Tools hi-fi, the platform surface these agents live in. One connection manager for every source the agents may touch, a connection step that treats credentials as a first-class moment, and the operator's console where the chat, the contact stream and the token spend sit on one screen.

The connection manager, the operator console with its live metrics, and the first step of connecting a database.

Outcome & reflection

Kodabase was specified end to end, four agents, five screens, a four-week build plan for a two-person team, with the interaction model settled before any of it was written.

What I would carry into any AI product from this: the valuable design decision is almost never the answer, it is the moment before the answer. Deciding what the system is not allowed to assume is the whole job. Two clarifying questions cost the user twenty seconds and are the difference between a number they can act on and a number they will quietly stop trusting after the third time it is wrong.

Where the line sits matters. Code correctness is a testing problem, stress tests and a security pass catch it far better than a human reading diffs. Semantic decisions are not, because the ground truth is not in the codebase. Designing an AI product is largely deciding which of the two kinds of uncertainty you are looking at, and refusing to solve one with the other's tool.

The part I would push harder on now: the clarifying questions are designed, but nothing in the spec measures whether people answered them or abandoned at them. I would instrument that first, a question the user skips is a question that was not worth asking.

Next case study

LawVerse →
All work 07. Legal tech · AI product

LawVerse

A legal research assistant that is allowed to say "I don't know". Every answer carries the page it came from, and the page number is the one thing the model is never permitted to write.

Product DesignerAI interaction · Trust · VerificationWeb appKolabs
The problem

In legal work the failure that matters is not a wrong answer. It is a fluent wrong answer.

A general model will name a doctrine, attribute it to a jurist and cite an article number, in exactly the register a lawyer expects. When the underlying fact is not in its weights, the output does not collapse into obvious nonsense. It degrades into plausible nonsense: a real-sounding article that does not exist, a holding that inverts the actual one.

So the product question was never accuracy. It was verifiability. A lawyer cannot check an answer that does not say where it came from. They either trust it or redo the research, and an answer that cannot be checked has saved nobody anything. It has only created the impression that the question is settled.

The hard part

The first version used an off-the-shelf assistant with file search. Retrieval was a black box: no control over how the book was cut up, no page mapping, no way to see what the model had actually been shown. You could not debug an answer because you could not see its evidence.

Rebuilding retrieval as part of the product, rather than as an implementation detail, is what made the interface honest. Three constraints came out of that, and they are product decisions before they are engineering ones:

One. The model sees only text retrieved from the corpus. Its own legal knowledge is not a permitted source. Two. Every claim carries a page number and a verbatim excerpt, so it can be checked against the physical book. Three. When retrieval finds nothing usable, the model is never called at all. A fixed refusal is returned instead.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

The page number is not something the model is allowed to say

The model returns integers pointing at the numbered passages it was given. The application resolves those integers to page numbers and excerpts recorded when the book was ingested. Any index outside the valid range is dropped without comment.

Trade-off The model can still misattribute, cite passage 7 while paraphrasing passage 12. What the system guarantees is that a cited page is a real page containing the excerpt shown. Closing the remaining gap needs per-claim checking, which is on the roadmap and honestly named as such.
DECISION 02

Refusal is a feature, and it happens before the model runs

If nothing relevant comes back, there is no generation call. The user gets a fixed sentence saying the corpus does not cover the question, with no citation block underneath it.

Trade-off The product looks less capable in a demo. It is the difference between a research tool and a confident stranger.
DECISION 03

Two ways of searching, because legal questions come in two kinds

Conceptual questions ("when someone accepts the risk of killing") defeat keyword search. Terms of art and article numbers defeat meaning-based search, which places related concepts near each other and cannot tell "next to" from "is". Both run, and the results are merged by rank rather than by score.

Trade-off Two searches per question instead of one, and the latency to match. Merging by rank was chosen precisely because the two scoring systems have no common unit, so any weighted blend would be a tuning knob that drifts as the library grows.
DECISION 04

The evidence is frozen at the moment the answer was given

The excerpt shown under an answer is copied into storage when the answer is written, not looked up later. The library can be re-ingested or replaced. An answer from six months ago still shows the text it was actually built from.

Trade-off Duplicated text and storage that grows with use. Reviewing an old answer has to mean reviewing the evidence behind it, not the library's current state.
What the user sees
Dolo eventual occurs when the agent, without directly intending the result, foresees it as possible and accepts it. It is distinguished from conscious negligence, where the agent foresees the result but sincerely believes it will not occur.
Fontes
p. 412 · o agente prevê o resultado como possível e, ainda assim, assume o risco de produzi-lo, anuindo com a sua ocorrência
p. 87 · na culpa consciente há previsão do resultado, mas o agente confia sinceramente que ele não ocorrerá

Two sources, two page numbers, two verbatim excerpts. The excerpts are long enough to notice a mismatch without opening the book, which is the whole point of showing them.

The product

Captured from the application running locally. The corpus, the retrieval database and the generation key are not in these screens, so the answered state below is drawn rather than photographed.

Where the trust is built

The interface has three states, and designing the boring one properly is what makes the good one credible.

Answeredanswerpage numbersexcerptstime taken
Refusedfixed sentenceno citation block at all
Failedsystem writes its own failure messageclient reloads rather than inventing an error

The third row is the one people skip. Exactly one reply is written for every question asked, even when the pipeline breaks, so the transcript is never a question with nothing under it. The client is built to trust that and refetch, instead of drawing an error bubble the server does not know about.

Outcome & reflection

LawVerse runs against a single 1,000-page reference work and answers in Portuguese with page-level citations, or refuses. The interface makes both outcomes look deliberate, which is the part I care about.

What I would carry into any AI product from this: decide which field must never be generated, and then make it structurally impossible to generate. Not a prompt instruction, not a validation warning. A path the model has no access to. Here the model's only output on that path is a small integer, and every value of it resolves to a page a deterministic extraction actually recorded. That is why a LawVerse page number cannot be invented, and it is a design decision rather than a technical one.

What I am not satisfied with: the system proves that a cited page is real, not that it supports the sentence next to it. That gap is named in the roadmap rather than papered over, and the excerpt is the honest partial mitigation. There is also no measurement of how often people actually open a citation, and a citation nobody opens is decoration.

Play-Kolabs →
All work 08. Research platform · Simulation

Play-Kolabs

A research platform for artificial brains under instrumentation. Characters with memory, chemistry and a body, running whether or not anyone is watching, with a measurement on every tick.

Product owner & designerSystems design · Simulation · InstrumentationEngine & web clientKolabs
The problem

Every AI character product shares one failure. The character is a paragraph in a prompt. It gets re-summarised into the context window each turn, so it has no state that survives the model's attention. It cannot be surprised, it cannot change its mind about you across ten sessions, and it stops existing between your messages.

That is not a model problem. It is an architecture problem, and it is the reason these products feel hollow after twenty minutes.

The premise

Move the character out of the prompt and into a database, then ask the model to narrate what that state implies rather than to be the character.

A character here is a graph of memories with weighted associations, eight hormone levels, a body carrying blood glucose, sleep debt and inflammation, a document of social and emotional state, plus habits, senses, beliefs with confidence values and multi-axis relationships.

This inverts the cost model, and that is the finding worth stating plainly: simulating the world is free. Only the player's typed turns cost anything.

Key decisions
DECISION 01

The background world makes zero model calls

Off-screen characters do not call a language model. Needs decay, chemistry steps, actions are chosen by a utility competition, habits form, memories are written and forgotten. All of it deterministic, all of it offline, all of it free.

Trade-off Every behaviour has to be modelled explicitly instead of being conjured by a prompt. It is much more work up front, and it is the only reason a hundred characters can keep living at no cost.
DECISION 02

Instrumentation is the product, not a debug view

One telemetry row per character per tick. Hormones, body state, chosen action, memory writes. The web client exposes it directly: live brain panels on the character sheets and a 3D view of the memory graph you can walk through.

Trade-off Storage grows fast and the interface is far more complex than a chat window. An artificial brain you cannot inspect is a claim, not a result.
DECISION 03

Determinism where it can be deterministic

Roughly 47,000 lines of engine, 19,000 lines of tests, two runtime dependencies. Memory, emotion, physiology and social dynamics are ordinary typed code. Language is the only part delegated to a model.

Trade-off No emergent magic from a bigger model. Reproducible runs, testable behaviour, and results that mean something because the same input gives the same output.
DECISION 04

The same engine answers a research question

Generate a fictional organisation with staff, give an agent a real work task, then vary that agent's biology and working conditions and measure the deliverable. Sleep debt, glucose and inflammation feed a work-quality signal that can be compared across runs.

Trade-off It is a simulation, so it evidences the model rather than the world. Stated as a scenario-testing instrument, not as a claim about real people.
The product

Captured from the engine running locally against a real save. The narration model was switched off, so what the cast shows is the deterministic side of the engine: needs decaying, actions chosen, no model involved.

How it is put together
Memory

Nodes with embeddings, importance, valence and arousal, joined by weighted associative and inhibitory edges. Memories decay and are forgotten.

Chemistry

Eight hormones modulating regions of a brain model, which in turn gate which action wins the utility competition on a given tick.

Body

Blood glucose, oxygen saturation, heart rate, sleep debt, inflammation. Physiology feeds back into how well the mind works.

Society

Social perception passes and a registry of emotional appraisals, producing relationships that move on several axes at once.

Player turnone narration callperceptionappraisalmemory write
Every tickneedschemistryaction choicehabitstelemetry row
Clienttranscript and living castcharacter sheets3D memory graphnote vault

The top row is the only row that spends anything. Everything on the second row runs on a timer, in one process, for free.

Outcome & reflection

The engine runs. Characters accumulate memory across sessions, revise their opinion of you, sleep badly and carry it into the next day, and the whole state is visible rather than asserted.

What this taught me about designing with AI: the interesting decision is almost always what you refuse to hand to the model. Here the model does one job, putting language on a state it did not compute. Everything that has to be consistent, inspectable and reproducible was kept in code. That is the same principle as the citation path in LawVerse, arrived at from a completely different direction.

Where I would push next: the instrumentation proves the simulation is internally consistent, not that it is a good model of anything. Deciding what would count as validation is the honest open question, and it is a research question rather than a product one.

All work Research · Motivational psychology & product

Motivations & Technology

A cross-framework study mapping eight core human drives across the major motivation models, and onto the product mechanics each one actually justifies.

Synthesis of 10 published frameworksGamificationApplied to product design

Gamification usually arrives as a bag of tricks: points, badges, leaderboards. This study asks the harder question, which human motivation is a given mechanic actually serving, and what do the established psychological models say about it?

The method

The study sets eight columns, eight underlying human needs, and then aligns every model against them. Octalysis and Marczewski's player types sit on that axis alongside Maslow, Herzberg, McClelland, Alderfer, Locke, Sirgy, Max-Neef and the Sexy Canvas. Instead of treating these frameworks as competing, it treats them as different lenses on the same eight needs, and the alignment is where the insight lives.

Octalysis, 8 core drivesMcClelland, affiliation, power, achievementAlderfer, ERG Herzberg, motivator vs hygieneSirgyMaslow Locke, goal settingMax-Neef matrixMarczewski (Andrzej), player typesFour basic motivations

The Herzberg axis is the one that changes design decisions most. Splitting the drives into motivators: which create positive feeling when present, and hygiene factors: which only create negative feeling when absent, tells you which mechanics grow engagement and which merely prevent churn. Scarcity, loss avoidance and social pressure sit on the hygiene side. Purpose, accomplishment, creativity and ownership sit on the motivator side.

A mechanic that removes pain is not the same as a mechanic that creates desire. Most products confuse the two.

The eight columns

The columns are not one framework relabelled. Each one is a position I defined, and then aligned every model against: Octalysis and Andrzej Marczewski's player types sit on the axis alongside Maslow, Herzberg, McClelland, Alderfer, Locke, Sirgy, Max-Neef and the Sexy Canvas. Ten models, one axis, 80 mapped cells.

Underneath each column sits the layer that makes it usable: 87 applied mechanics: what technology actually does to reach that drive, and which of those I would refuse to ship.

It also documents the mechanics I would not ship. Streak-loss anxiety, countdown pressure, public shaming of late contributors, pay-to-restore, they work, which is exactly why they need to be named. Writing only the flattering half of gamification would make this a sales brochure rather than a study.

The matrix

Eight drives across the top, and three different layers of information underneath, the competing theories, the mechanics each drive justifies, and the psychology behind it. Switch the layer to cross-read the same eight columns three different ways.

Rows are competing models of motivation. Read a column downwards to see one drive named in seven of them.

Layer01Meaning & Purpose02Progress & Accomplishment03Creativity & Feedback04Ownership & Possession05Social Influence06Scarcity & Impatience07Curiosity & Unpredictability08Loss & Avoidance
McClelland, three needsAffiliationPowerAchievementAchievementAffiliationAchievementPowerPower

Scroll the table sideways to see all eight drives.

The Herzberg row is the one that changes decisions. Drives 01–04 are motivators: purpose, accomplishment, creativity and ownership build real engagement when added. Drives 05–08 are hygiene factors: social pressure, scarcity, unpredictability and loss aversion mostly punish their own absence. A product leaning on the second group can grow fast and still feel hollow.

Try it: build a motivation map

A matrix is only useful if it produces decisions. This turns it into one, choose a client profile, a business goal and an audience, and it ranks the drives to design for, names the mechanics that express them, and flags when the mix is leaning on pressure rather than value.

Interactive

Motivation map builder

Built from the matrix above. Choose one option per row.

The eight drives

DRIVE 01

Meaning & purpose

The need to serve something larger than yourself, a mission, a vocation, a community. The user believes their actions contribute to something that matters.

In the wildWikipedia editors and open-source contributors doing sustained, demanding work for no payment at all.

DRIVE 02

Progress & accomplishment

The internal drive to develop skill and overcome challenge. The most-exploited drive, because points, badges and leaderboards are the easiest mechanics to build. Feedback has to be tangible and constant.

In the wildDuolingo, points, badges, levels and relentless feedback on a visible skill curve.

DRIVE 03

Creativity & feedback

Testing creative capacity and seeing the results of it. Offering expression isn't enough, the output must be visible and answerable. This is where evergreen mechanics come from: systems that stay alive without new content being added.

In the wildMinecraft, endless construction, no content updates required to stay engaging.

DRIVE 04

Ownership & possession

Once a user feels they own something, they want to improve it and won't abandon it. Accounts that cost time and effort to build are almost never walked away from.

In the wildInstagram, a profile that took years to build carries a switching cost no competitor can match.

DRIVE 05

Social influence & relatedness

Mentorship, acceptance, companionship, but also competition and envy. Humans are not only social but impressionable, and want to impress. Groups adopt shared markers to be recognised.

In the wildFandoms on Twitter, coordinating hashtags, group purchases and boycotts as a single organism.

DRIVE 06

Scarcity & impatience

Wanting something because it can't be had yet. Anticipation converts into attention: if people can't get it now, they think about it all day. Scarcity sells, particularly when framed as access rather than product.

In the wildClubhouse, invite-only launch, with invitations changing hands for real money.

DRIVE 07

Curiosity & unpredictability

When something falls outside the brain's pattern recognition, attention locks on. Unpredictability makes us wonder what happens if we stop, which is precisely why we don't.

In the wildThe infinite feed, the next item might matter, so the scroll never resolves.

DRIVE 08

Loss & avoidance

Acting to prevent something negative, or to avoid forfeiting a positive. The fear that stopping now makes everything invested so far worthless.

In the wildTrials that deliver partial value for days, then require payment to complete what you started.

From drive to mechanic

The second half of the study is a catalogue of mechanics filed under the drive each one serves, so a designer can start from the motivation they need and select the mechanic, rather than starting from a mechanic and hoping. It covers, among many others, evergreen mechanics, glowing choice, the sunk-cost tragedy, elitism and group pride, social treasure, fixed intervals and commitment dynamics, mini-quests, rolling rewards, mystery boxes and random drops, beginner's luck, chain combos, countdowns, easter eggs, FOMO, status-quo sloth, water-cooler moments, moats, obvious wonders, the scarlet letter, boosters, social prods, the aura effect, conformity anchors and the oracle effect.

Why this matters in product work

It replaces "let's add points" with a defensible chain: which need are we serving, which model supports it, which mechanic expresses it, and what does it cost the user.

Where I've used it

Directly in Next Day's challenge system and in AVAIA's learning loop, and as the basis for the essay on motivation in education.

The full study is a mapped matrix, each drive against every framework, with concept, explanation, example and mechanics. Available on request.

All work Essay · Education & product

Motivation in modern education

Why students disengage, what Wikipedia and Waze reveal about intrinsic motivation, and how the Socratic method becomes a product loop.

Essay (unpublished)Basis for AVAIAPortuguese

"Why am I learning this?" is the most honest question a student ever asks, and the point where curiosity either catches or goes out.

The disengagement

The essay opens with a student who loves fashion and design, and switches off the moment the lesson turns to the Second World War. Not because she lacks interest, but because nobody drew the thread between what she loves and what she's being asked to learn. Without that connection the attention circuit simply closes. Curiosity is born of personal relevance. Where there's meaning there's curiosity, and where there's curiosity there's memory.

The paradox

Then it turns the problem over. Imagine being asked to monitor hundreds of forum pages, correct every error, keep everything current, unpaid. Most people would refuse outright. Yet thousands do exactly that every day on Wikipedia. They aren't working for free. They're exercising an interest. The person maintaining the Star Wars page is a Star Wars obsessive. That's intrinsic motivation: autonomy, because they chose it, and competence, because they know the subject.

People aren't working for free. They're exercising an interest.

The collective interest

Waze is the second case. In 2011, millions tolerated navigation apps that routinely sent them the wrong way. Waze reframed the task: not "get from A to B" but "join us to defeat the traffic monster together." Contribution stopped being data entry and became participation in a shared cause, and users built the routing system themselves. Google bought it for $1.1 billion. The lesson: humans commit to narratives in which they have an active role.

The Socratic method

Plutarch had the principle nineteen centuries ago, educating is not filling a vessel but lighting a flame. The Socratic method inverts the lecture: the teacher doesn't dispense answers, they construct questions that make the student think, question and discover. When a student reaches an answer by reflection rather than instruction, the reward is neurological, and learning stops being a task and becomes personal discovery.

Three pillars

Storytelling

The student has to understand why this is relevant to them. Connection comes from the tutor engaging with their individuality, what they feel, think, and want.

Activity cycle

Activity can't be one-off. Each round must produce a reward, even if the reward is understanding, and lead into the next. A quest without a loop gets abandoned.

Objective

The student must see the endpoint, and it should feel large, something they'd have assumed was out of reach, now visibly within it.

In a conventional classroom this is where frustration lives: one teacher cannot connect the Pythagorean theorem to thirty different sets of interests simultaneously. Most students memorise. Far fewer leave knowing when and how to apply what they memorised.

How it became a product

The essay closes by turning the three pillars into AVAIA: not a replacement for the teacher but an assistant that gives each student an individual AI tutor. Storytelling becomes the Connection feature, using a student's own interests to build relevance. The activity cycle becomes a concrete loop, topic, introduction, chat, quiz, reinforcement, where the tutor uses analogies and short questions rather than supplying answers, and restarts the loop with a different approach whenever the quiz shows the idea didn't land. And the objective becomes epic meaning: proving that knowledge isn't imposed from outside but is a tool for understanding what the student already loves.

From your world to the subject, and from the subject, back out to the world.
Written, not published. The full essay is in Portuguese and available on request.

The full study, eight core drives, ten frameworks, and the mechanics each one justifies.

6 chaptersOriginal synthesisSee the matrix & tool →
Motivations & Technology
Chapter 1 of 6
Contents
Chapter 01

Why frameworks, not tricks

Gamification usually arrives as a bag of tricks. Points, badges, a leaderboard, bolted onto a product in the hope that engagement follows. Sometimes it does, briefly. Then it stops, and nobody can say why.

The reason is that a mechanic is not a motivation. A leaderboard is an expression of something, the desire to progress and be seen progressing. If your users don't carry that desire, the leaderboard is furniture. Worse, if you attach the wrong mechanic to the wrong need, you can actively repel the people you were trying to keep.

This study starts from the other end. Instead of asking "which mechanics should we add," it asks "which human motivations are actually in play here", and only then, "what expresses that."

The method

The spine is the eight core drives from the Octalysis framework. Onto that spine, each of the major models of human motivation is mapped: McClelland's three needs, Alderfer's ERG, Herzberg's motivator–hygiene split, Sirgy's model, Maslow's hierarchy, Locke's goal-setting theory, Max-Neef's matrix of needs, and Marczewski's player types.

These frameworks are usually taught as rivals. Treated as lenses instead, they stop competing and start triangulating: the same eight underlying needs, described in eight different vocabularies. Where they agree, you can design with confidence. Where they disagree, you've found something worth thinking about.

Chapter 02

The eight core drives

Every drive below is stated three ways: what it is, why it works on people, and where it already exists in a product you know.

01 · Meaning & Purpose

The need for a larger significance, to fulfil a purpose, to have been chosen for something that matters. The user believes their action serves something bigger than themselves. It's the hero complex, and it makes people feel useful.

Seen in: Wikipedia editors and open-source contributors, doing sustained, demanding, unglamorous work for no payment at all.

02 · Progress & Accomplishment

The internal drive to make progress, develop skill, and eventually overcome challenge. This is the most exploited drive in the industry, because it's the easiest to build for, most points, badges and leaderboards live here. The condition is that feedback must be tangible and constant. A system where skill can always improve, and where improvement is visible.

Seen in: Duolingo, points, badges, levels and relentless feedback against a visible curve.

03 · Creativity & Feedback

Testing creative capacity, then seeing the result of it. Offering a way to express creativity is not enough on its own, the output has to be visible and answerable. Purely open-ended play eventually exhausts itself. Something must happen in response. This is the origin of evergreen mechanics: systems that stay alive without the designer continually adding content.

Seen in: Minecraft, endless construction, no content updates required to remain engaging.

04 · Ownership & Possession

The motivation of possessing. Once a user feels they own something, they naturally become attached and want to improve it. Accounts that cost time and resources are almost never abandoned, and there's a display dimension too: ownership as a way of showing superiority through aesthetics.

Seen in: Instagram, a profile built over years carries a switching cost no competitor can match.

05 · Social Influence & Relatedness

Everything social: mentorship, acceptance, companionship, social response, and also competition and envy. When you see a friend who is excellent at something, you're pulled toward that level. Humans are not only social but impressionable, and want to impress. Being like others, or having what your peers have, is a way of not being alone.

Seen in: fandoms, coordinating hashtags, group purchases and boycotts as a single organism.

06 · Scarcity & Impatience

Wanting something precisely because you can't have it. If people can't get it now, they think about it all day. Anticipation converts into attention. Scarcity sells hardest when framed as access rather than product. VIP for those who "can."

Seen in: Clubhouse, an invite-only launch, with invitations changing hands for real money.

07 · Curiosity & Unpredictability

When something falls outside your brain's regular pattern recognition, attention locks onto the unexpected and returns to it. Unpredictability makes us wonder what might happen if we stopped, which is exactly why we don't.

Seen in: the infinite feed. The next item might matter. It usually doesn't. The scroll never resolves.

08 · Loss & Avoidance

Acting to prevent something negative, or to avoid forfeiting a positive. Admitting that everything you've done so far was wasted, because you're stopping now, is harder than continuing. Opportunities are disappearing, and if you don't act immediately you lose the chance for good.

Seen in: trials that deliver partial value for days, then require payment to complete what you already started.

Chapter 03

Motivator or hygiene

Of all the mappings in this study, the one that changes decisions most is Herzberg's. He divides factors into two kinds that behave asymmetrically.

  • Motivators produce positive feeling when they are present. Adding them adds something.
  • Hygiene factors produce negative feeling when they are absent. Adding them mostly removes a pain you created.

Mapped onto the eight drives, the split falls cleanly. Drives 01–04, meaning, progress, creativity, ownership, are motivators. Drives 05–08, social influence, scarcity, curiosity, loss, are hygiene factors.

Why this matters commercially

The hygiene drives are seductive because they move numbers fast. Scarcity, FOMO, streak loss and social comparison all produce immediate, measurable behaviour. But they work by manufacturing discomfort and then selling relief from it. A product built mainly on that foundation can grow quickly and still feel hollow, and users leave the moment a gentler alternative appears, often without being able to explain why.

The motivator drives are slower and harder to instrument. They also produce the retention that doesn't need defending.

The practical rule

Use hygiene mechanics for urgency, never for the core loop. If a product's three strongest drives are all hygiene factors, that's not a strategy, it's a warning.

Chapter 04

The frameworks, mapped

Each drive read through every model. The value isn't in any single row. It's in reading a column downwards and seeing one need named eight ways.

McClelland, three needs

Affiliation, power and achievement. Meaning and social influence resolve to affiliation. Progress, ownership and scarcity resolve to achievement. Creativity, curiosity and loss resolve to power, the desire for control.

Alderfer, ERG

Existence, relatedness, growth. Meaning sits alone in growth. Progress, creativity, ownership and social influence live in relatedness and esteem. Scarcity, curiosity and loss fall back to existence, safety, and at the far end, physiology.

Sirgy

Splits along commitment versus satisfaction. The first five drives sit on the engagement side, esteem, actualisation, aesthetics and knowledge, the social. The last three collapse into safety, which is satisfaction rather than engagement: necessary, not motivating.

Maslow

Meaning is self-actualisation. Progress straddles actualisation and esteem. Creativity and ownership are esteem. Social influence is the social tier. Scarcity, curiosity and loss are safety, with loss reaching down into the physiological.

Locke, goal setting

Rather than a tier, Locke gives a chain: values, goals, actions, results, feedback. Each drive reorders that chain. Meaning starts at values. Progress starts at goals. Creativity starts at actions. Loss starts at results. Where a drive enters the chain tells you where its mechanic must intervene.

Max-Neef, matrix of needs

Freedom, identity, creation, idleness, participation, affection, protection, subsistence, understanding. This is the most humane of the models and the least commercial, useful precisely because it refuses to reduce a person to a user.

Marczewski, player types

Philanthropists, Achievers, Free Spirits, Consumers, Socialisers, Self Seekers, Exploiters, Networkers, one per drive. This is the layer that turns the study into a targeting tool: identify the dominant type in your audience and you know which drive leads.

Chapter 05

The mechanics catalogue

The second half of the study files mechanics under the drive each one serves, so that a designer can start from the motivation and select the expression, rather than starting from a mechanic and hoping.

Meaning & Purpose

Narrative context. Elitism through clan, guild or class, which inspires group pride. Humanitarian hero. Higher meaning, gifts that normally cost money, given in a way that ties to a larger theme. Beginner's luck. Free lunch. Destiny child, the dreams you had, now visibly possible. Co-creator.

Progress & Accomplishment

Points. Badges on their own. Ranking and leaderboards. Progress bars. Quest lists. Winning a differentiated prize among competitors. Plus five, correct behaviour, appropriate reward. Coronation. Level-up symphony: positive sound for positive action.

Creativity & Feedback

Milestone unlocks. Evergreen mechanics. General carrot, a goal plus the tools and methods to strategise toward it. Real-time control. Chain combos. Instant feedback. Boosters. Blank-space filling. Voluntary autonomy.

Ownership & Possession

Virtual goods. Building from scratch. Collection sets. Avatars. Earned lunch. The learning curve itself. Protection. Recruitment. Monitoring.

Social Influence

Friending. Social treasure, rewards only another player can give you. SeeSaw bump. Group quests requiring a whole team. Bragging. Water cooler. Thank-you economy. Mentoring. Social prods, minimum-effort interaction, one click.

Scarcity & Impatience

Appointment dynamics, pre-announced or recurring windows in which the desired action must happen. Fixed intervals. Prize pacing, creating scarcity while raising the value of an eventual win. Countdowns. Accelerators. Moats, randomly generated challenges demanding real skill.

Curiosity & Unpredictability

Glowing choice, which makes users feel clever. Mini-quests. Visual storytelling. Easter eggs. Random rewards, loot and drops. Mystery boxes. Rolling rewards. Obvious wonders, things always there that you suddenly see.

Loss & Avoidance

The sunk-cost tragedy, continuing an activity that stopped being enjoyable, to avoid the feeling of having wasted it. Progress loss. FOMO. Disappearing opportunity. Status quo sloth, engaging loops that harden into habit. Scarlet letter, the fear of falling behind and being left out. Visual grave, making defeat clear while offering a hook back.

Chapter 06

Using it in practice

The study is only worth the pages if it produces decisions. In practice it runs as four questions.

1. Who is actually here?

Identify the dominant player type. An audience of Achievers and an audience of Philanthropists want opposite things from the same screen, one wants to be measured, the other wants to matter.

2. What is the business actually asking for?

Acquisition, habit, contribution, monetisation, learning, community. Each pulls a different set of drives to the front, and being honest about which one you're serving prevents designing for all six badly.

3. Which drives does that combination select?

Profile, goal and audience together rank the eight. The top three are where design effort belongs. The rest are noise for this product, at this moment.

4. Is the mix honest?

Count the hygiene factors among the leaders. One is healthy, it supplies urgency. Two or more means the product is being built on pressure, and should be rebalanced toward a motivator before it ships.

The interactive builder on the research page runs exactly this logic, and returns the mechanics catalogue filtered to the drives it selects.

Where I've used it

Directly in Next Day's challenge system, sponsor-backed challenges are meaning and social influence, with scarcity supplying the deadline. And in AVAIA's learning loop, where the Socratic cycle is progress and creativity, deliberately avoiding the loss mechanics that make educational products feel punitive.
